title: 2026-05-20-technical-deep-dive-opentelemetry-token-metrics
summary: Redwood SE team walked Silverline through recommended OpenTelemetry instrumentation for token-level metrics, tracing the inference lifecycle (ingest -> routing -> batching -> kernel execution -> response). Discussed cardinality concerns, sampling, metric naming, dashboards in Redwood Console, and VPC/on-prem collector deployment. Agreed next steps: share OTEL example configs, provide a test endpoint with token-metrics enabled, run a 24h benchmark and follow up with dashboard templates.

transcript:
[00:00] Liam: okay good afternoon everyone thanks for joining, I'm Liam Carter from Redwood, with Priya and Marco from the SE team. um can folks introduce quickly?
[00:08] Jared: hey this is Jared Kim, head of ML at Silverline Financial, Anita is our platform lead, Tom is security.
[00:14] Anita: hi all, thanks for running this.
[00:17] Priya: great thanks, quick agenda: we want to run through OpenTelemetry integration options, token-level metrics, what to expose to Prom/Grafana vs traces in the OTEL backend, and how Redwood Console can map those into dashboards.
[00:29] Tom: quick ask on security side — we need to understand trace retention, PII scrubbing, and whether the OTEL collector can run entirely in our VPC / on prem.
[00:38] Marco: yes absolutely, we have patterns for private collector, and all sensitive attrs can be redacted at the collector. we'll show config examples.
[00:45] Priya: high level, for inference we recommend instrumenting three signals: distributed traces for request lifecycle, metrics for aggregates (qps, latency p50/p95), and token-level counters/histograms to reason about cost and model behavior.
[00:59] Jared: token-level metrics — can you clarify what you mean? do you mean every token emitted increments a counter? that sounds high-cardinality and expensive.
[01:08] Priya: good question. by token-level metrics we mean counters and histograms at the request granularity: tokens_generated_total (increment by tokens), tokens_input_total, and token_latency_histogram (per-token generation latency), plus derived rates. we don't recommend label-per-token or storing raw token text.
[01:26] Anita: okay so labels would be route/model/quantization profile or customerId? what's safe?
[01:33] Marco: recommended labels: model_name, model_version, route_id, deployment_zone, and customer_tier. avoid user_id or prompt text. for per-customer multi-tenant needs we suggest hashed customer_id or tenant_id with coarse cardinality.
[01:49] Tom: and KV cache metrics? we need to see hit rate per route to understand tail latency improvements.
[01:56] Priya: yes we expose kv_cache_hit_count and kv_cache_miss_count, and kv_cache_hit_rate calculated via rate(). also we recommend batch_size_histogram which helps tune batching params.
[02:07] Jared: how do these maps into traces — do you put token events as spans?
[02:12] Priya: in general we avoid per-token spans; that's too chatty. instead trace spans should represent stages: ingress span, routing span, batch-join span, kernel_exec span (which can have attributes like batch_size, seq_len, kv_cache_hits), and emit token-level metrics separately as metrics. if you need token-level debug traces you can enable a sampled debug trace with token attributes for a tiny percentage.
[02:35] Speaker 1: (muffled) yeah sampling is critical.
[02:38] Marco: one common pattern — use span events to mark milestones (first_token, last_token) which are low-cardinality and useful for latency breakdowns without high cardinality.
[02:48] Anita: what's the recommended sampling strategy for traces? we have high volume production.
[02:52] Priya: default: head-based sampling for errors + tail sampling for long-tail latency. combine 1% uniform sampling for non-error traces plus 100% sampling for error traces and traces above 95th percentile latency. OTEL Collector supports tail-sampling with a storage backend.
[03:08] Jared: tail sampling sounds heavy; we need storage. can Redwood help operate that?
[03:12] Liam: for hosted customers we can offer a managed tracing backend, but for private deployments you run the collector and tracing backend in your VPC. we provide config templates and can help set up an internal Jaeger/Tempo or use datadog/SignalFx integrations.
[03:25] Tom: retention — how long do you typically keep spans and token metrics?
[03:29] Marco: metrics are usually cheap — we recommend Prometheus/Thanos or Cortex for longer retention (90 days+). spans are larger; typical retention is 7-30 days depending on compliance. we can tune retention and sampling to meet your constraints.
[03:44] Jared: about dashboards — can Redwood Console display token-level metrics natively or do we need to pull from Prom/Grafana?
[03:51] Priya: Redwood Console can ingest and surface token-level metrics if you forward them to the Console or to your metrics backend and then wire them in. we provide dashboard templates (token throughput, kv_cache hit rate, batch size distribution, per-route latency p50/p95). we'll share JSON templates you can import to Grafana or the Console.
[04:07] Anita: are there best practices for metric names and units?
[04:10] Priya: use a stable naming scheme: redwood_tokens_generated_total (counter, tokens), redwood_token_latency_seconds (histogram), redwood_kv_cache_hit_rate (gauge 0-1), redwood_batch_size (histogram). include units in the metric name or doc.
[04:25] Jared: sample config?
[04:27] Priya: yes Priya: we'll share an OTEL Collector config that shows receivers, processors (batch/spanprocessor/attributes), exporters to Prom and to your tracing backend, plus attribute redaction rules for PII. link: https://redwood.example/docs/otel-samples (note: placeholder link)
[04:44] Tom: question on VPC/on-prem — network egress: can the collector keep everything within our VPC? we can't have traces leaving.
[04:51] Marco: yes, collector and exporter can be inside your VPC, and you can upload metrics to your Prom/cortex inside VPC. for private Redwood deployments we also offer an option to ship metrics to your observability stack only, not to our control plane.
[05:03] Anita: how do we correlate user requests from our front-end tracing into the inference traces? we want end-to-end correlation.
[05:09] Priya: propagate traceparent (W3C) and set resource attributes like service.name and deployment.zone. Redwood will accept incoming tracecontext headers and include them in spans. you can also tag spans with request_id and session_id (hashed) to correlate without exposing PII.
[05:23] Jared: any advice on high-cardinality labels — e.g. route + model_version + quantization_profile + customer_env — could explode.
[05:31] Marco: limit cardinality by preferring coarse labels and using label values like model_family instead of full commit hashes. if you need more dimensions, use logs/traces with sampling or push aggregated labels into metrics via relabeling at the collector.
[05:45] Priya: also consider using exemplar linking from histograms to sampled traces — that gives a direct route from metric bucket to example trace without high-cardinality metrics.
[05:54] Anita: good — can you show a quick dashboard sample?
[05:58] Priya: sure, slide share/ screen (brief silence while screen is shared) — you can see tokens_per_request, tokens_generated_per_minute, kv_cache_hit_rate over time, batch_size histogram, latency p50/p95.
[06:15] (screen noise)
[06:18] Priya: highlight — batch_size histogram and kv_cache_hit_rate together tell you if you're losing batching opportunities due to small seq_len or hot-sharding.
[06:28] Jared: what's the overhead of emitting token metrics? per-token counter increments will cost CPU/IO.
[06:33] Marco: we implement lightweight in-process counters that aggregate to per-request metrics and flush at request completion; avoid synchronous network calls per token. if you push to prometheus via pushgateway or OTEL exporter, batch sending reduces overhead. measured overhead is typically <1-3% CPU at moderate qps but depends on sampling.
[06:51] Tom: quantization — does that change the metrics we should collect?
[06:54] Priya: yes add a quant_profile label on model_version or an explicit metric redwood_quantization_profile{bits="8"} so you can slice latency/cost by quantization. also kernel-level metrics like flops_estimated or kernel_exec_time_seconds help when comparing int8 vs fp16 performance.
[07:11] Jared: example of a span breakdown — can you show attributes we should include?
[07:15] Priya: attributes: request_id, model_name, model_version, batch_size, seq_len, kv_cache_hits, route_id, deployment_zone, error (if any), first_token_time, last_token_time. keep attributes low-cardinality.
[07:29] Speaker 1: (typing)
[07:31] Anita: can we see the sample OTEL YAML now?
[07:33] Priya: yes pasting briefly — receiver otlp, processors batch, attributes processor to drop prompt_text, exporters prometheus/selfhosted. we'll share full file.
[07:45] Jared: for the benchmarking test you mentioned — what should we run?
[07:50] Liam: recommended: 24h of mixed workload: 60% short chat style requests (seq_len <128), 30% medium (128-512), 10% long (>512). capture tokens_generated_total, token latency hist, p50/p95 inference latency, batch size distribution, kv cache hit rate, and tail sampling of traces.
[08:06] Marco: also collect kernel_exec_time by model variant and quantization profile so you can measure perf/cost tradeoffs.
[08:14] Jared: and if we run this in our staging, what do you need from us?
[08:18] Liam: we need access to a staging endpoint (we'll provision one) and a short script to generate the workload. we'll share a k6/postman helper and the OTEL config.
[08:27] Anita: compliance — Tom will enumerate retention windows and redaction rules.
[08:31] Tom: yes I'll send that.
[08:34] Priya: a few gotchas: 1) avoid including raw prompt_text or completions in spans/attributes; 2) avoid per-token spans; 3) watch metric labels cardinality; 4) consider exemplar linking for histograms.
[08:48] Jared: anything specific for on-prem GPU infra?
[08:52] Marco: yes, make sure the OTEL collector has sufficient memory for tail-sampling if you enable it. also prefer local storage for buffering to handle bursts. set resource limits for the collector container.
[09:03] Anita: if we want the collector to forward to both internal Prometheus and Redwood Console, can it do dual export?
[09:08] Priya: yes the collector can have multiple exporters. we usually send to internal long-term metrics backend and to Redwood for quick sanity dashboards; use relabel rules to drop sensitive labels for external exports.
[09:20] Jared: will Redwood provide dashboard templates?
[09:22] Liam: yes we'll provide both Grafana JSON and Redwood Console templates.
[09:27] Anita: timeline-wise we want to get this into staging this week.
[09:30] Priya: action list recap: we'll send the OTEL collector config, sample workload script, and dashboard templates. you'll deploy collector in staging, run 24h benchmark, then we'll review.
[09:42] (crosstalk)
[09:44] Liam: any other questions on metrics naming or cost?
[09:48] Tom: question on encryption keys for telemetry traffic? can we use mTLS?
[09:52] Marco: yes OTLP supports TLS/mTLS. we can provide examples for mutual auth to ensure collectors only talk to your backends.
[09:59] Jared: ok sounds good. thanks everyone.
[10:01] Priya: thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[10:04] Liam: end — quick recap of next steps and owners in chat.
